name: Guanche

ancestors.notes: Wikipedia (Guanche language): most linguists propose Guanche was likely a Berber language, or at least genealogically related to Berber, within Afroasiatic; the affiliation is a hypothesis, not a settled classification, hence the reduced weight.

notes: STUB. Guanche, the extinct language (or dialect continuum) of the pre-Hispanic Guanche people of the Canary Islands, spoken until the 16th-17th century when the population was assimilated following the Spanish conquest. No native written corpus survives at any scale sufficient to reconstruct an orthography or a reliable phoneme inventory: what is known comes from a handful of words and phrases recorded by early modern geographers/travellers, place names, and Guanche lexical survivals in Canary Islands Spanish, all transmitted through ad hoc Spanish-based transcriptions of varying reliability rather than a native script or a standardised transliteration. There is therefore no citable grapheme-to-IPA mapping to assert; graphemes is left empty rather than inventing a Latin placeholder inventory, per the hard rule against fabricating an orthography for a poorly-attested language. The Berber-family hypothesis (weak but the mainstream position) is recorded as the sole ancestry link so this stub has a real parent rather than a graph hole.
